title: Why I don't "believe in science."
summary: Educated Barbarian philosophy episode, a follow-up to his critique of science-based fitness. Drawing on Nietzsche's 'We Scholars' (Beyond Good and Evil ch. 6), he argues that science is a fragile, human-run method that money, politics and morality corrupt into 'scientism', a cult of belief. His answer is constant skepticism and owning your own experience, not rejecting science.
claims: His previous video argued that science-based fitness has become disconnected from reality and needs a reality check

Science is the systematic study of the physical and natural world through observation, experiment and testing theories against evidence; for a result to count, the variables must be defined so the study can be replicated
The scientific method has seven steps: question, research, hypothesis, experiment, data analysis, conclusion, communication
Philosophy is the father of science; both aim at truth through logic
One person observing something produces experience, not evidence; you may share your experience but you cannot call it scientific evidence
Absolute truth may not exist, but searching for it is what progress is; humanity stagnates whenever it stops searching properly
Science beats religion completely for explaining the material world, while religion is better suited to the spiritual; humans need both
Because science is produced by subjective humans, it is fragile and always close to corruption by money, politics or morality; only competence and constant vigilance protect it
Industry-funded studies (soy, dairy, poultry, eggs and cholesterol, pharma) reliably reach conclusions that favour their funders, because they start from the conclusion and work backwards
Telling people not to question the science is itself unscientific; science has to stay open to having its origins questioned
He defines scientism as trusting the methods of natural science so much that you stop checking them, so the 'truths' they produce become wrong
For any idea in your head you can google a study that seems to support it
Scientism was inevitable: most people want black-and-white answers, so science adapted to its public, even though a proper study should contain more unknowns than certainties
Most people read only a study's abstract and conclusion, never its methods, so they have no way to judge whether the conclusion is sound
Starting from a belief (e.g. 'I like watermelon') and then finding a study to confirm it is scientism, not the scientific method
Scientists who take criticism of scientism as an attack on science (his example is a Daniel Dennett quote) are showing scientism's cult-like defensiveness
Needlessly complex scientific jargon works like Latin mass: it keeps laymen dependent on an authority to interpret for them
Most fact-checking institutions are funded by government, so taxpayers pay to be told what to think
Asking 'source?' online is usually a way to dismiss a claim without debating it, and any source you give gets rejected as not reputable enough
'Believe in science' is a contradiction: once you believe instead of checking, no science is left, only scientism
Signs like 'science is real' are virtue signalling that empties science of content and actually breeds distrust of science
The answer is not to become anti-science and go backwards, but Nietzsche's middle path: accept your own subjectivity while still pursuing objectivity
Do not blindly worship scientific authorities; someone who really thinks scientifically wants you to understand things before you apply them
If science allies with the state, it risks producing an authoritarian technocracy; he gives the COVID lockdowns and job-linked vaccine mandates as a thinly veiled example
The cure is to keep questioning science at every turn and never let anyone deny your own experience; people who reject all criticism of science are the real anti-science crowd
